after: Submitted by Dan Sonsie, founder and evidence custodian

before: This submission supports proportionate competence and accountability requirements where evidence establishes material risk, a limitation in existing controls and an incremental public benefit. It distinguishes minimum trade competence from advanced residential capability and preserves evidence-based career progression. The choice of regulatory mechanism should follow the function, evidence and implementation test.
after: I am Dan Sonsie, founder of Carpenters for Housing Reform Victoria and a practising carpenter with approximately 20 years’ experience. This submission draws on my firsthand carpentry experience and longstanding informal discussions with industry colleagues; it does not claim their formal endorsement or to represent every Victorian carpenter.

before: The scheme should establish a credible minimum carpenter standard without assuming that entry registration demonstrates every capability required in complex residential renovation. Victoria should preserve the capacity to test whether a distinct advanced capability gap exists. An endorsement, revised existing class, additional class, non-statutory credential or no additional mechanism should remain available until the relevant scope, consumer problem, assessment reliability and legal consequences are established.
after: The scheme should establish a credible minimum carpenter standard without assuming that entry registration demonstrates every capability required in complex residential renovation. This initiative proposes Registered Residential Carpenter (RRC) as a candidate for a bounded advanced-capability pilot. The pilot should test the need and benefit before wider rollout. An endorsement, revised existing class, additional class, non-statutory credential or no additional mechanism remain alternatives; the final statutory vehicle is not predetermined.

before: The Department should publish the comparison and explain why the selected model is proportionate to the verified risk. This would allow stakeholders to assess both the scope coverage and the regulatory burden of the final proposal.
after: Interstate schemes provide useful comparisons. NSW recognises carpentry contractor licences and separate supervisor certificates for defined work. Queensland provides a carpentry licence class and contractor-type licences permitting direct contracts within licensed scope, with additional business and financial requirements. Compare their scope, role boundaries, burdens and available outcome data when designing a Victorian pathway. These published rules do not establish pilot results or prove reduced defects; their permissions and thresholds do not apply in Victoria. [18–19]

before: Victoria should preserve a credible carpenter career pathway: apprenticeship and baseline trade competence, appropriate additional requirements for independent business operation, and optional assessed progression for defined residential work where need and public benefit are demonstrated. Do not require the full builder pathway for every narrower function if a proportionate lawful alternative can meet the same consumer outcome. Existing builder entry pathways remain directly available; advanced recognition must never become mandatory before builder registration. An endorsement, reform of DB-L Carpentry, optional RRC, a non-statutory credential or no additional mechanism remain options. Additional statutory contracting authority would require an authorised mechanism, not merely a voluntary credential.
after: Proposed RRC pilot and collaboration. I propose working with DTP and the BPC to design a bounded trial of additional residential capability, with defined scope, lawful permissions, oversight and evaluation before wider rollout. I offer to take a lead role in its development and delivery alongside a government-supported team, with appointments and resources determined by government and appropriately independent evaluation. Test work quality, consumer outcomes, costs, access and boundary decisions against a baseline and relevant alternatives, including existing pathways. Modify, narrow or discontinue the pathway if the evidence does not support it. The pilot would not itself grant statutory authority or commit government funding.

before: These materials are capability-first and vehicle-neutral. They do not presume that RRC is the preferred regulatory mechanism, do not criticise current DB-L practitioners, and do not claim government or regulator endorsement.
after: These working materials remain capability-first and adaptable to different regulatory mechanisms. This submission proposes RRC as a candidate for a bounded pilot, without predetermining the eventual statutory vehicle, criticising current DB-L practitioners or claiming government or regulator endorsement.

before: If the evidence justifies minimum trade regulation, implement it with clear competence, authority, transition and evaluation arrangements. Preserve advanced residential capability as a subsequent, bounded evidence question and a potential career progression pathway. If recognition is justified, define its function, scope, assessment and controls before choosing the title or statutory vehicle. If existing pathways or less restrictive measures address the problem, retain them.
after: I support baseline residential carpenter registration in principle, with government still needing to justify its scope, cost, assessment and transition arrangements. I offer practical collaboration to develop and evaluate a bounded RRC pilot for additional residential capability. Define its function, scope, assessment, lawful authority and controls before wider rollout. Retain alternative mechanisms and existing builder pathways; change or discontinue the additional pathway if the evidence does not support it.
